analysis.one_liner: Lets licensed gun dealers sell firearms, including handguns, across state lines following only the seller's state law.
analysis.headline: The House never voted on it: the bill was referred to the Judiciary Committee on June 7, 2006, and died there when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current federal law, a licensed dealer can sell a rifle or shotgun in person to someone from another state only if the sale is legal under the laws of both the dealer's state and the buyer's state, and handguns generally cannot be sold in person to out-of-state buyers at all. This bill would rewrite that rule so a cross-border sale is governed only by the law of the dealer's state, and it would cover all firearms, handguns included. That would let residents of states with strict gun laws buy guns in neighboring states under the neighboring state's looser rules. The bill never advanced past its first referral to committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Licensed firearms dealers gain the most: they could sell to out-of-state customers after checking only their own state's rules instead of reconciling two states' laws, and they could sell handguns in person to nonresidents, which current law does not allow. Some individual gun buyers in states with strict gun laws would also gain, because they could shop in a state with looser rules.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Licensed gun dealers and out-of-state buyers

how_it_helps.text: Interstate in-person sales by licensed dealers would be governed only by the state where the dealer does business, rather than the laws of both states as current law requires.

The bill extends the cross-border in-person sales provision from rifles and shotguns to all firearms, which would for the first time allow licensed dealers to sell handguns in person to buyers from other states.

analysis.who_pays: States with stricter gun laws bear the cost: their residents could acquire guns, including handguns, in neighboring states while bypassing their home state's rules, and their police and courts would face guns in circulation that their own laws were written to keep out. The public in those states bears the safety risk.
analysis.who_pays_short: Residents of states with stricter gun laws

drawbacks.text: A handgun sale that is legal in the dealer's state but barred in the buyer's home state would become lawful, undercutting a state's ability to set and enforce its own gun rules.

Even a supporter would acknowledge the trade: simpler one-state compliance for dealers comes at the price of weaker home-state oversight of who is buying guns, and the bill's expansion to handguns is a larger change than the title suggests.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The convenience is real but narrow — dealers filing paperwork under one state's law instead of two. The cost is broader: it shifts the governing rules for gun sales to whichever state is laxest, which matters most to states that deliberately set stricter standards, and the quiet extension to handguns is a bigger policy change than the bill's name advertises. Weighed honestly, this mostly benefits dealers and lax-state commerce at the expense of stricter states' laws.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee took no action on it before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Rick Renzi introduced the bill on June 7, 2006, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day.
The action history shows no further steps — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.
The bill would have changed the rule that interstate in-person sales by licensed dealers must comply with the laws of both states, replacing it with the dealer's state law alone.
Sixteen members cosponsored the bill, fifteen Republicans and one Democrat.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: States with stricter gun laws and the current dual-state rule came out ahead, since the federal law governing cross-border gun sales, including the bar on in-person handgun sales to nonresidents, remained unchanged. The dealers and buyers who would have gained a wider market got nothing.

for.name: 1 of 201 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill — the bill's only Democratic supporter.

against.name: F. James Sensenbrenner
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; the committee held no hearing or vote on it before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Fifteen of the sixteen cosponsors were Republicans and one was a Democrat, and the bill died in committee without ever reaching the floor.

industries.note: The bill frees dealers from having to comply with the buyer's home-state law and lets them sell handguns in person to out-of-state residents, expanding their customer base. The expanded sales come precisely from buyers whose own states' rules would otherwise block the transaction, so the dealer gain is the stricter states' loss.

A wider legal market for handgun sales across state lines would increase demand flowing through licensed dealers. The added volume would come largely from sales that current law and stricter state laws channel differently.
